papers.title: What Makes Online Content Viral?
papers.study_kind: Observational field study plus randomized vignette experiments
papers.scope: News homepage/email-list virality, plus advertising, customer-service and injury-story experimental vignettes; not writing quality or comprehension. PDF is ahead-of-print © 2011; publisher issue is 2012.
papers.sample_and_design: 6,956 NYT homepage articles Aug 30–Nov 30 2008 observed every 15 minutes; 20% reached most-emailed list. A random 2,566 received human ratings from independent groups of three per construct; uncoded values set to standardized mean with dummy. Day fixed-effects logistic models control placement and other factors. Experiments randomize story versions for amusement (N=49), anger (N=45) and sadness (N=47).
papers.outcomes: Field outcome binary ever appeared on most-emailed list, not direct individual sharing rate; experiments 1–7 self-reported sharing likelihood and arousal; no comprehension.

findings.claim: One standard deviation higher rated anger associated with 34% higher odds and awe 30% higher odds of list entry in model 4.
findings.denominator: 6,956 field articles; 2,566 human rated, rest mean-imputed with indicator
findings.interpretation_limits: Associations conditional on model; percentage odds, not percentage-point probability or causal response.

findings.claim: Randomized high vs low amusement: sharing likelihood 3.97 vs 2.92; high vs low anger 5.71 vs 3.37 on 1–7 scale.
findings.interpretation_limits: Different vignettes change substantive facts as well as emotion; intention, not observed sharing.

findings.claim: High vs low sadness: sharing likelihood 2.39 vs 3.80 and arousal 2.75 vs 3.89, 1–7.
findings.interpretation_limits: Changes injury context and title; mediation analysis is model-based, not randomized arousal.

findings.claim: All three manual raters per construct, alpha > .70; 2,566 randomly sampled articles scored, remaining imputed at standardized mean.
findings.interpretation_limits: High agreement is construct-specific; imputation and coder emotional response do not establish individual reader response.

limitations: NYT homepage and most-emailed ranking in 2008; access and prominence affect opportunity to share.
High arousal anger, anxiety and awe versus low-arousal sadness differs from positivity/negativity; not all emotion or negative content has one direction.
Experimental article versions differ in material events; assigned texts can cause stated response differences, but emotion/arousal mediation is not independently randomized.
The physical PDF shows 2011 ahead-of-print; publisher labels first online 2012.
data_or_code_leads: Web appendix referenced in source pp.3–4, 9; availability/rights not verified.
extraction_issues: Figure 2 reports fitted probability changes; narrative uses odds; do not substitute one for another.

papers.title: Narrative Style Influences Citation Frequency in Climate Change Science
papers.scope: English climate-change research abstracts, 2009–2010, 19 high-output journals, cited at least once; citation count is a proxy rather than tested comprehension.
papers.sample_and_design: 802 raw, 732 after quality control; seven crowd ratings per abstract by 155 contributors; six narrativity indicators, PCA plus regressions; minority ratings on first-person test removed and binary means rounded.
papers.outcomes: Web of Science total citations as of 30 March 2016, log transformed; not experimentally assigned style or reader outcomes.

findings.claim: Narrativity index vs log citations R²=.05; index journal-mean vs log journal impact factor R²=.62.
findings.denominator: 732 selected abstracts from 19 journals; second analysis uses journal means
findings.interpretation_limits: Weak individual relationship; journal-level association is not individual causal effect.

findings.claim: Conjunctions rho=.211; connectivity rho=.171; sensory rho=.138; appeal p=.0037. Setting p=.36 and narrative perspective p=.32.
findings.interpretation_limits: Univariate associations; p values not effect sizes and correlations do not show narrative causes citation.

findings.claim: Journal ANOVA R²=.43; selected model using year, PC1, log authors and log impact factor R²=.41.
findings.evidence_locator_or_snippet: Non-narrative variables and Multiple Linear Regression
findings.interpretation_limits: Final model uses impact factor rather than journal identity; journal confounding remains. No direct randomized test.

findings.claim: Each abstract initially received seven judgments; 155 total contributors; 802 to 732 post-quality-control.
findings.interpretation_limits: Excludes zero-citation articles; filtering entire coder responses based on first-person majority can remove disagreement.

limitations: Six broad proxies for narrative include conjunctions, explicit connections and recommendations that are not uniquely stories or chronological narration.
Different journals and editorial selection are strongly linked to both narrativity and citation; paper itself says it could not test mechanisms.
Excludes zero-citation articles, narrow climate field and era, abstracts rather than complete texts.
Authors sometimes use causal language; study supports association only.

data_or_code_leads.resource: Official PLOS supplements S1 Text instructions and S2 Text questions
data_or_code_leads.inspected: Read both: yes/no setting, narrator self-reference, and appeal/action; counts of sensory/emotional language, causal/contrast/temporal conjunctions, and links to preceding sentence. Six dimensions are not the project narrate function.
data_or_code_leads.reuse: Reuse questions as scoped examples and preserve raw judgments and disagreement; do not equate ratings with paragraph function.

data_or_code_leads.resource: Official PLOS raw judgment CSV, R script and journal data
data_or_code_leads.inspected: Complete CSV aggregate: 5,614 raw judgment rows, 802 unit IDs, exactly seven rows per ID. Raw/pre-QC, not 732 post-QC abstracts. R script read as text only: groups by unit, filters to first-person-question majority, aggregates judgments and filters publication year; not executed. Journal CSV receipt records 19 rows.
data_or_code_leads.reuse: Possible provenance-backed multi-rater methodological comparison, not a reproduced analysis or independent evidence of causality; keep sensitive metadata and abstracts out of derived outputs.

extraction_issues: Local physical PDF pages coincide with printed 1–12; word hyphenation split in extraction.

supplement_access.unit_and_privacy: Raw rows include sensitive contributor and source-text fields; only aggregate counts and instrument descriptions retained here.
supplement_access.validation_limit: Inspected instructions, questions, raw CSV aggregate, and script as text; no analysis executed or replicated.

papers.title: Style, content, and the success of ideas
papers.study_kind: Observational predictive analyses plus randomized one-sentence experiments
papers.scope: Five social science fields from selected JSTOR journals, plus online volunteer ratings of isolated research descriptions; citations or perceived importance/impact, not measured actual learning.
papers.sample_and_design: 28,774 research articles, 1990–2018; nine LIWC function-word category rates as style features, LDA topic mixture as content proxies, journal/year and other controls; negative-binomial and neural-network models. Exploratory section-level analyses. MTurk personal voice experiment N=185 and Prolific tense experiment N=234.
papers.outcomes: Google Scholar citation counts observationally; randomized experiments 1–7 perceived importance and expected impact, not actual citations.

findings.claim: Adding style features adjusted R² .208 to .217 in negative-binomial model; neural model predicted R² .209 to .234. Authors express gains as 4–11% of model-explained variance, not 4–11% of all variance.
findings.interpretation_limits: Topic controls and function words are proxies, not clean separation of all content and style; model comparison is predictive, not causal.

findings.claim: Exploratory first-person coefficients: front end b=.076 p<.001; empirical middle b=−.029 p=.016; conclusion b=.007 p=.29.
findings.denominator: Article corpus; section analysis, exact eligible denominator not explicitly given in text
findings.interpretation_limits: Adjusted negative-binomial coefficients, not percentage citation change; section classification and confounding remain.

findings.denominator: Article corpus; exact section denominator not stated
findings.interpretation_limits: Preposition and article frequency is not comprehension; direction varies by section; p for middle article is nonsignificant.

findings.claim: Personal-voice randomized condition vs control: importance 6.15 vs 5.76 and expected impact 5.97 vs 5.39, on 1–7 scales.
findings.interpretation_limits: One sentence, perceived outcomes, not citation or comprehension; treatment changes subject framing.

findings.claim: Present vs past condition: importance 5.97 vs 5.60 and expected impact 5.69 vs 5.20, on 1–7 scales.
findings.denominator: 234 Prolific participants per Method; reported impact F(1,200) has inconsistent denominator
findings.interpretation_limits: One sentence; changes tense/aspect and perceived currentness, potentially factual meaning. Printed mediation paragraph incorrectly names personal voice.

limitations: Function words carry grammatical and semantic meaning: pronouns change attribution and agency, tense/aspect changes temporal state, prepositions and negation scope. Topic mixture cannot isolate content quality or novelty; authors acknowledge this p.11.
Journal fixed effects and many controls reduce some confounding but do not remove unobserved topic quality, authorship or selection.
Section-level analyses are exploratory and paper reports null interactions; coefficients do not justify uniform first person or removal of articles/prepositions.
Study 3 and 4 manipulate a single vignette each and measure perceptions. Causal effect is for text versions and stated ratings only; mediators observational.
data_or_code_leads: Paper references supplementary S1–S9 and LIWC dictionaries, JSTOR source and Publish or Perish; full datasets and permissions are not established by this review.
extraction_issues: p.10 Study 4 uses personal voice in mediation paragraph despite a tense manipulation; reported F(1,200) for impact differs from N=234 and importance F(1,232). Preserve discrepancy rather than silently fixing.

cross_paper_synthesis: Sharing and citation are context-bound measures of diffusion; neither is evidence of reader comprehension, factual accuracy or author satisfaction.

P08 and P12 use different citation samples and different feature constructions; shared topic is not independent replications of a paragraph function or narrative intervention. P12 itself cites P06 as prior work.
Arousal and valence are distinct; neither emotion nor positivity is a universal writing target.
Function words are style indicators in P12, not semantically empty in an actual edit; grammar contributes reference, polarity, time and scope.

proposed_rule_changes.scope_trigger: Author supplies a relevant experience or a concrete example advances the stated purpose.
proposed_rule_changes.proposal: Offer a sourced scene or example as one optional route, preserving origin and distinguishing observation from invention; never require a narrative opening.
proposed_rule_changes.expected_benefit: Makes an abstract relationship recoverable while preserving choice and voice; benefit remains to be tested for this audience.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A technical reference entry needs a precise definition or lookup, not an invented story.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Record provenance, author approval, and links to the illustrated claim.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic_or_author: Whether the case illuminates the point and the author wants its tone.

proposed_rule_changes.scope_trigger: A revision changes tense, reference, article, preposition, modality or attribution.
proposed_rule_changes.proposal: Protect temporal state, scope, actor and technical meaning; show alternatives rather than optimizing pronouns, grammatical word counts or tense for citation prediction.
proposed_rule_changes.expected_benefit: Preserve factual meaning and author voice while giving agency and temporal framing contextual attention.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: Changing had to has can imply continued relevance or a different time relationship; removing a preposition can lose a condition.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Compare tokens and declared preserved phrases; flag changes to protected terms and tense as review candidates, not errors.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic_or_author: Determine whether meaning changes, and whether chosen voice serves the task.

proposed_rule_changes.scope_trigger: A claim, example, evidence or inference is present.
proposed_rule_changes.proposal: Retain target links and ask whether the evidence supports the particular claim and whether inference exceeds it.
proposed_rule_changes.expected_benefit: Supports source fidelity and meaningful connected reasoning.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A highly shared emotional anecdote may illustrate experience but cannot establish population frequency or prove a claim.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Check links and provenance fields resolve; count only supplied annotated evidence.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic_or_author: Judge evidential relevance, inferential scope and whether explanation helps reader.

proposed_rule_changes.scope_trigger: A tool proposes changing prose to maximize sharing, citation counts, sentiment or low readability score.
proposed_rule_changes.proposal: Treat these as optional user-declared outcomes with testable tradeoffs, not proxies for good writing, comprehension or accuracy.
proposed_rule_changes.expected_benefit: Avoids sacrificing meaning, learning goals and voice for an indirect popularity measure.
proposed_rule_changes.counterexample: A safety notice may rightly express low-arousal uncertainty and specialist terminology while serving its audience.
proposed_rule_changes.mechanical: Record declared purpose and inspect counts as descriptive data only.
proposed_rule_changes.semantic_or_author: Author chooses objectives; reader studies measure comprehension or task success directly.

github_reuse.common_infrastructure: GUM eRST relation graphs and discourse-crosswalk.json; argument corpora link evidence and claim targets; retain labels, spans, uncertainty and rights, not semantic equivalence.
github_reuse.plausible_differentiator: An author-controlled adapter can preserve source labels, expose exact target links and voice constraints, and invite contextual comparison of alternatives.
github_reuse.demonstrated_advantage: None established; 36-item calibration and imported crosswalks do not validate reader outcomes, voice preservation or superiority.
github_reuse.missing_evidence: Test reader understanding, factual fidelity, perceived author voice and task completion with independent raters or readers; annotations are not outcome measurements.

open_questions: Can readers recover the target claim, story-to-idea connection and evidence strength without changing author intent?
Do voice-preserving alternative drafts improve comprehension or task performance for the specified audience?
What citation or reach goals, if any, has the author explicitly prioritized and what constraints govern them?
